author: Al Jazeera English
description:
The Sudanese pound has lost more than 90 percent of its value since war broke out between Sudan’s army and the Rapid Support Forces in April 2023.

The currency collapse has contributed to soaring prices for basic goods, putting food and other essentials beyond the reach of many families.

The Central Bank’s decision to float the pound has added further pressure, while Sudan’s heavy reliance on imported goods means many businesses must pay for supplies in hard currency.

Families living on fixed salaries describe having to drastically reduce spending on essentials, including food, milk and cooking oil.

Shop owners are also struggling as the cost of importing goods rises and consumers have less money to spend.

The economic crisis is compounding the devastating humanitarian consequences of Sudan’s war, which has displaced millions of people and disrupted livelihoods across the country.

Al Jazeera's Heba Motgan reports from Khartoum, Sudan

Jamal fled his home in Khartoum, travelled to Al-Jazira and then crossed into South Sudan before reaching Uganda by land.
He says Uganda provided safety and became a second home, but despite having 34 years of engineering experience, he was unable to find work.
Now, he believes parts of Sudan are safe enough for his family to return, despite knowing that conditions will not be as they were before the war.
He hopes to find work repairing and rebuilding infrastructure damaged by the conflict, while giving his children the opportunity to return to school.
Jamal Mubarak tells his own story from Seeta in Uganda’s Mukono district.

description:
More than 1,000 medical and health graduates have protested in Baghdad, demanding government jobs amid high youth unemployment in Iraq.

The demonstrations near the Finance Ministry have reportedly been met with police violence, with protesters describing the use of batons and electric shocks during what they say were peaceful protests.

Iraq has long relied heavily on government employment, leaving many young graduates competing for a limited number of public-sector positions. Youth unemployment is reportedly around twice the national average of 15 percent.

The demonstrations are raising concerns among Iraqi authorities about a possible return of the mass protest movement that swept across the country in 2019.

That movement was driven in part by unemployment, corruption, poor public services and demands for political reform.

With many of those underlying economic problems still unresolved, the latest protests highlight the growing frustration among Iraq’s young graduates.

Al Jaze

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
It's been two weeks since floods swept through communities in the Himalayas. When a section of Langtang Lirung mountain and the glacier above it collapsed, millions of cubic metres of rock and ice fell more than a kilometre to the valley below. The impact registered as a magnitude 5.2 earthquake. The mass of debris travelled more than 14 kilometres in seven minutes towards the China-Nepal border crossing, which was obliterated. The surge of melting ice, rock and sediment then plunged down the Trishuli valley, gathering more water and gouging chunks out of the riverbank. Workers on site filmed its approach before fleeing, but hundreds of others were buried. The avalanche swept away bridges, buildings and entire villages, carrying boulders bigger than cars. Within an hour, it had left a trail of devastation stretching more than 50 kilometres, while flooding continued south for more than 100 kilometres. 

Al Jazeera's Daniel McKerrell explains.

Subscribe to our channel: http://bit.ly/AJ
title: How a Himalayan avalanche unleashed a trail of destruction across Nepal
